1	# lerp — scope
2	
3	Lerp is a small, reliable CLI, written in Go, that orchestrates software
4	work through Linear. You put tickets on a board; lerp runs coding agents
5	to move them across it.
6	
7	This document is the fence around the project. It exists because lerp's
8	predecessor died of bloat — the code and the conceptual framework grew
9	until nobody could hold the whole thing in their head. Lerp is the
10	opposite bet: a tool whose every layer one person can understand, whose
11	surface area stays small enough to be elegant, and whose workflow is a
12	well-lit path, not a cage. When a proposal conflicts with this document,
13	the proposal loses or the document is amended — deliberately, never by
14	drift.
15	
16	## The model
17	
18	**Linear is the database.** All durable state — what work exists, what
19	stage it is in, who has claimed it, what was decided — lives in Linear.
20	Lerp keeps no store of its own: no SQLite, no journal, no server.
21	
22	**The board is the DAG.** A queue is a Linear status with instructions
23	attached. Workflow topology exists only in where tickets sit and where
24	queues point; lerp never contains an `if` about your process. Routing is
25	done by placing a ticket: a big feature enters at Planning, a small fix
26	enters at Implementing. Branching is a human or an agent moving a
27	ticket, never config syntax.
28	
29	A hop on the board is a decision somebody makes. Iteration is not a
30	decision: a stage that hands work back to an earlier one draws a cycle,
31	and bounding a cycle needs a round count — state outside Linear, or an
32	`if` about your process. So bounded iteration happens inside a single
33	queue run, where the count is the agent's own context and the board
34	never hears about it. Review-and-fix is the worked example: it lives in
35	the implement prompt, and only what the loop could not settle comes back
36	to a human as a move.
37	
38	**Lerp is a reconciler.** Desired state is the board; actual state is
39	the agent processes running on this machine. Lerp runs one loop:
40	compare the two, then start, adopt, or reap agents until they match. A
41	crash — of an agent, of lerp, of the laptop — is not an error case; it
42	is drift, and the loop repairs drift.
43	
44	Lerp is not privileged. Humans, agents, and Linear's own automations
45	(a merged PR advancing a ticket) may all move tickets; the loop
46	reconciles whatever board it finds, without caring who changed it.
47	
48	That neutrality has a price, and it is the one thing lerp requires of
49	a board: **lerp needs the status field on the teams it serves.** A
50	stage finishes by moving the ticket, so an automation that moves it
51	*during* a stage takes that move away — the loop respects what it
52	finds, and the stage's `on_success` hop simply never happens. The
53	merged-PR case above is benign because it fires after the pipeline is
54	done with the ticket; Linear's git automations that fire while a pull
55	request is open are not, and opening a pull request is what an
56	implement stage does. Nothing in lerp can resolve that collision
57	without becoming privileged, so it is a condition of use rather than a
58	defect: on a served team, the triggers that fire mid-stage are set to
59	No action — or, deliberately, at a status the pipeline itself names,
60	which makes the automation the next stage's trigger rather than the
61	thief of the last one's hop. Lerp reads the served teams' automations
62	at startup and names the mid-stage ones that point somewhere the
63	config does not.
64	
65	## The five concepts
66	
67	Lerp's entire ontology. Each is a noun a new reader can learn in a
68	sentence.
69	
70	1. **Ticket** — a Linear issue. The unit of work. Lerp never invents
71	   work items of its own.
72	2. **Queue** — a Linear status with four fields of config: the status,
73	   a prompt, a runner, and the status to move to on success (optionally,
74	   on failure). Nothing else. No conditionals, no templating logic, no
75	   DAG syntax. On a clean exit, lerp moves the ticket only if the agent
76	   didn't — `on-success` is the default, not a verdict. An agent
77	   escalates, branches, or refuses by moving the ticket itself; lerp
78	   respects whatever it finds. A ticket blocked by an unfinished ticket
79	   (Linear's `blockedBy`) is not eligible for pickup, no matter what
80	   queue it sits in — blocking relations are how humans sequence
81	   concurrent work.
82	3. **Runner** — an adapter to a coding-agent CLI (Claude Code, Codex,
83	   Antigravity, …). The contract: takes a prompt and a working
84	   directory, runs to exit, exit code means done or failed. The
85	   contract is the lowest common denominator — a capability every
86	   runner can't offer is a capability lerp doesn't have. The adapters
87	   for the CLIs lerp knows ship built in — one file per vendor, holding
88	   the flag spellings and the session bookkeeping a command template
89	   cannot express — and config names one and overrides its defaults.
90	   The command runner remains for everything else: any line of shell
91	   whose exit code keeps the contract is a runner, adapter or not.
92	   Which runner serves a queue is one word of that queue's config,
93	   never a policy: lerp does not rotate, prefer, or fall back between
94	   runners. Choosing who does the work is routing, and routing is a
95	   human placing something — a ticket on a status, a word in a queue's
96	   config.
97	4. **Lane** — a concurrency unit. Lerp runs at most N agents at once.
98	   N is small — small enough that one person can watch what is
99	   happening — and the number itself is a default the operator
100	   overrides per run, not a constant this document pins. A lane's
101	   occupant is a run: a pid, a log file, a ticket, and a workspace
102	   (see invariant 9).
103	5. **The loop** — the reconciler described above. There is exactly one.
104	
105	Amendment rule: adding a sixth concept requires removing one of these
106	five. If that trade is unappealing, the feature is out of scope.
107	
108	## Invariants
109	
110	1. **Linear is the only durable store.** Local disk holds config,
111	   the operator's credentials, evidence of running processes, and run
112	   telemetry, nothing else. Losing all local state may cost compute;
113	   it may never cost correctness. `rm -rf .lerp/runs` under live
114	   agents means orphaned processes and re-run stages — never lost or
115	   corrupted tickets. Telemetry is the deliberate fourth resident: an
116	   append-only file of finished-run measurements — tokens, cost,
117	   duration, outcome — written once at run exit and read by nothing in
118	   the loop. It is history, not state: losing it costs a chart, never
119	   a ticket.
120	
121	2. **Team → repo is a function** (many-to-one allowed, not a
122	   bijection). Every ticket must resolve to exactly one working
123	   directory. Two repos may not claim the same team; one repo may serve
124	   several teams (the monorepo case falls out for free). At startup,
125	   lerp verifies the function and refuses to run if it doesn't hold.
126	
127	3. **Every queue run is safe to kill and restart from its beginning.**
128	   Progress is checkpointed only at queue boundaries, as artifacts in
129	   Linear (a plan in the ticket, a PR link, a verdict comment). Lerp
130	   never checkpoints inside a run. Kill anything at any time, on any
131	   machine; the worst case is a re-run stage.
132	
133	4. **The claim is the assignment, and the lock is in Linear.** Picking
134	   up a ticket means assigning it to the operating developer's Linear
135	   user. Claim protocol: assign to self, settle, read back; if the
136	   assignee is you, you won, otherwise walk away. The race window that
137	   remains resolves to duplicated compute, which invariant 3 already
138	   tolerates. No lerp server, no coordination service, ever.
139	
140	   Lerp is nobody on the board: it authenticates **as the operator**,
141	   so "assigned to Sarah" means Sarah. Two credentials do that, and
142	   both are Linear's own API, invariant 8 intact — a personal API key
143	   in `LINEAR_API_KEY`, which remains supported, or a token from
144	   `lerp login`: OAuth with `actor=user`, a PKCE public client, no
145	   service of lerp's standing behind it. (Login's loopback socket is a
146	   port exception, not a service; see "What lerp is not".) What stays
147	   out is an app or agent *actor*, work showing up as *lerp* rather
148	   than as a person: that would make the claim a lock held by a bot,
149	   and the board stop reading like a human team's. Lerp ships one
150	   public client ID, so a Linear application named lerp appears in the
151	   operator's authorized apps — a way to sign in as them, not a second
152	   party on it. All of which changes who signs the request, never what
153	   a claim means: the protocol above and the multiplayer semantics are
154	   untouched. The token itself is a credential, not a store and not a
155	   second layer of config — the operator's own, kept outside the
156	   clone, and neither constant nor irreplaceable: it expires and
157	   renews, either credential can be revoked in Linear, and losing the
158	   file costs a re-login, never correctness.
159	
160	5. **The engine is generic; the opinion ships as config.** Lerp's stock
161	   config encodes planning → human plan approval → implementing → a
162	   human merge, and the implement stage reviews its own work before it
163	   hands over. The engine knows nothing about that sequence — each queue
164	   is independent, and the topology exists only in the `on-success`
165	   pointers. The approval step is not engine either: it is a status no
166	   queue serves, where a ticket rests until a human promotes it.
167	
168	6. **Setup time and run time never mix.** `lerp init` (and humans) may
169	   create board structure — teams, statuses matching queues. The loop
170	   only moves tickets. A reconciler that edits its own board schema is
171	   how you get spooky action.
172	
173	7. **Durable = decisions; ephemeral = process.** Linear receives
174	   stage-boundary artifacts. The high-fidelity agent stream — every
175	   tool call and rationale — goes to a local log file, tailed live by
176	   the TUI and discarded without ceremony. Never post the firehose to
177	   Linear. A run's measurements — tokens, cost, duration — are process
178	   too, summarized: they land in the local telemetry file (invariant
179	   1), never on a ticket.
180	
181	8. **Lerp speaks exactly one external API: Linear.** Git, GitHub, and
182	   PRs belong to agents (via their prompts) and to humans. A PR is a
183	   stage-boundary artifact like any other — created by an agent with
184	   `gh`, attached to the ticket by Linear's GitHub integration, read
185	   by the next stage's prompt. Lerp never calls a code host and never
186	   inspects a branch. The engine that has never heard of PRs is the
187	   engine that works for people who don't make PRs.
188	
189	9. **Workspaces are provisioned by config, not by lerp.** A lane's
190	   workspace is created and destroyed by two config-supplied commands,
191	   provision and dispose; stock config uses git worktrees. Lerp invokes
192	   them with a unique lane/run identity (lane number, ticket id,
193	   workspace path) and otherwise knows nothing about what provision
194	   does. Environment isolation — ports, databases, containers — is the
195	   project's problem, solved inside its provision command. Lerp will
196	   never grow an isolation subsystem: no health checks, no readiness
197	   probes, no service definitions. If provision exits non-zero, the
198	   lane doesn't start and the ticket stays queued.
199	
200	## The interface
201	
202	TUI-first (Bubble Tea; lazygit is the spiritual reference). The TUI is
203	the engine — no daemon. Work happens while lerp is open; a headless
204	`lerp run` is the same loop without the chrome, if and when it earns
205	its existence.
206	
207	Two panels on one screen, one per question an operator actually has. The
208	list owns the screen: a main pane detailing the selected row opens beside
209	it with `enter` and closes with `esc`, and each panel remembers whether it
210	is open. An open pane is a surface the keyboard reaches — `tab` cycles the
211	panels and the pane the focused one has open, and the keys scroll it a line
212	at a time while it holds them — but it is a lens and never a third panel:
213	what it shows stays the selected row's business. Both start closed: a
214	ticket's detail is something you open once you have decided to read that
215	ticket, and a run's log is something you open to read that run — the work
216	row already says whether the run is alive without it. That is a display
217	default, not a rule about process.
218	
219	Above them sits a summary strip: each status the pass already read with
220	its ticket count, in board order. It is chrome, in the same class as the
221	status bar — a passive line over the list that was already fetched, not a
222	panel: it has no focus, no keys and no selection, and it drops off a window
223	that has no row to spare for it. Wanting it to answer to a key is a new
224	conversation, not an extension of this one.
225	
226	1. **Inbox** — what waits on a human: unclaimed tickets, and the
227	   operator's own claimed tickets, sitting in a status no queue serves —
228	   reviews to read, questions agents have raised, failed runs to retriage.
229	   It reads as a table, one row per ticket, and the Linear status is a
230	   column: the vocabulary is the operator's own, never a category invented
231	   here. It opens on what is blocked on a human — a failed run, a run
232	   finished at a gate, a ticket that left the pipeline — with the tickets
233	   that have not entered the pipeline yet standing as a summary line and
234	   reachable as a slice of their own: being blocked-on is an interrupt,
235	   pulling from the backlog is a sit-down motion. A claimed ticket resting
236	   in an intake status is never folded — no pass can pick it up again while
237	   the claim stands (invariant 4), so it is blocked on a human wherever
238	   Linear files it. Sorting it (by leverage, priority, status or project),
239	   scoping it to one project, searching it (`/`, a plain substring over the
240	   rows on screen) and slicing it to one status are display over the one
241	   list the pass already fetched — so the cycle offers only statuses that
242	   list already contains (Linear's unstarted and active categories),
243	   session-only, with no saved views and no filter syntax; filtering that
244	   changed *which* tickets were fetched would not be. Select a ticket, or a run of adjacent ones held with visual mode (`v`), and
245	   press `p` to promote it: pick a target from the configured queue
246	   statuses or a pipeline exit, and lerp moves it there. A promote into a
247	   status some queue serves also releases the claim the parked ticket was
248	   holding — an assigned ticket is never eligible, so keeping it would
249	   strand the ticket in a queue that could never pick it up. That release
250	   is invariant 4's protocol, not a second capability. Promote and
251	   force-start are the only writes the TUI makes anywhere.
252	2. **Work** — what the machine is doing with the board: one list,
253	   grouped by queue, holding the tickets running in each queue and the
254	   tickets waiting behind them. What is running and what runs next are
255	   the same question about the same tickets; the separate question is
256	   what needs a human. The main pane follows the selected row — a live
257	   log for a running ticket, what gates it for a waiting one — and opens
258	   on `enter` like the inbox's. Selecting a queued ticket and pressing
259	   `S` starts it now, past the lane limit.
260	   Force-start overrides exactly one thing, the lane count: the claim
261	   protocol still runs, a blocked ticket is still refused, and ordering is
262	   still not a keystroke — to change what runs *next*, move a ticket in
263	   Linear.
264	
265	One escape hatch: **eject**. Select a running ticket; lerp stops the
266	agent, frees its lane, and hands you the vendor's own resume command
267	(`claude --resume <session-id>`) so the headless run becomes your
268	interactive session, full context intact. Finish the work yourself or
269	toss the ticket back into a queue. Lerp does not implement
270	interactivity; it hands you the door.
271	
272	## Multiplayer
273	
274	Inherited from Linear, not built. Each developer runs their own lerp
275	against their own clone; a lockfile keeps it to one lerp per clone, and
276	invariant 4 arbitrates claims across machines. The board reads like a
277	human team's board — "Sarah has LERP-42 in Implementing" is true
278	whether Sarah or Sarah's agent is doing the work. Colleagues see claims
279	and stage artifacts, not each other's live streams — exactly the
280	visibility they have into each other's human work.
281	
282	No work stealing, no global scheduler, no fairness guarantees. Each
283	lerp fills its own lanes from what is unclaimed. A fifty-developer shop
284	that wants a scheduler wants a different product.
285	
286	## What lerp is not
287	
288	- Not a workflow engine: no conditionals, no DAG language, no plugin
289	  hooks. The board is the workflow.
290	- Not a process supervisor, CI system, or deployment tool.
291	- Not a server, daemon, or web service. Nothing listens on a port
292	  while lerp works. The one exception is `lerp login`: it opens a
293	  loopback socket on `127.0.0.1`, on an ephemeral port, for the
294	  seconds an OAuth redirect takes, and closes it before anything
295	  runs. No other command listens and the loop never listens, ever —
296	  login is setup time, which invariant 6 keeps on its own side of the
297	  line.
298	- Not a database. See invariant 1.
299	- Not an agent framework. Runners are subprocess adapters, not SDKs:
300	  lerp execs a vendor's CLI and reads what it prints. It never links
301	  an agent library, never calls a model API, never holds a
302	  conversation of its own.
303	- Not a Linear client, with one narrow exception: the inbox lists
304	  unassigned tickets in statuses no queue serves, promote moves a ticket
305	  the operator selected and settles its claim by the same rule a finished
306	  run uses, force-start claims a selected ticket through that same
307	  protocol, and the main pane reads that selected ticket's body and
308	  comments — lerp's own stage-boundary artifacts — read-only, never
309	  composing or replying, never navigating on to another ticket.
310	  Everything else — create, edit, comment, assign outside the claim
311	  protocol — stays in Linear.
312	- Not infrastructure for any other product to depend on. It is a
313	  standalone tool.
314	
315	## Not yet, maybe never
316	
317	Deferred consciously — none of these may sneak in as a subsystem:
318	
319	- Hang detection (pid alive, no progress) — timeouts, later, maybe.
320	- Live mid-run steering of agents — eject covers grabbing the wheel;
321	  revisit only if usage screams, and only within the runner contract.
322	- Headless `lerp run` — same loop, no TUI; wait until it hurts.
323	- Per-operator config layered over the repo's — the checked-in
324	  lerp.toml is the whole config, pipeline included, so the permissions
325	  it grants are versioned and reviewed and every developer runs the
326	  same pipeline. Repos share a pipeline by copying the file. A
327	  personal override or merge layer is complexity waiting for a reason.
328	- Runner policies — round-robin, prefer-then-fall-back. Each needs
329	  state no board holds, and each hides a failure a human should see.
330	  The question they answer — which vendor is better here — is one
331	  telemetry answers already, one config word at a time.
332	- A `lerp stats` view over the telemetry file. The file is the feature
333	  for now; `jq` is the dashboard. Wait until it hurts.
334	
335	## Litmus tests
336	
337	For any proposed change, in order:
338	
339	1. Does it add a sixth concept? Then which of the five does it remove?
340	2. Does it put durable state anywhere but Linear?
341	3. Does it make any queue run unsafe to kill?
342	4. Does it require a runner capability not all runners have?
343	5. Does it require lerp to speak to any API other than Linear?
344	6. Could it be config pointing at what exists, instead of code?
345	
346	A "yes" to 1–5 without an amendment to this document means no.
347
